notes.front: What is the Telemarketing Sales Rule (TSR)?
notes.back: The FTC's rule, in Title 16, part 310, of the Code of Federal Regulations, that implements the Telemarketing and Consumer Fraud and Abuse Prevention Act.
notes.explanation: It sets out deceptive and abusive telemarketing practices, record keeping, exemptions and the fee for the do-not-call registry, according to its table of sections.
notes.example: Like a highway code for sales calls: it says when, how and whom a telemarketer may call.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 310 (Telemarketing Sales Rule), 2026 edition, § 310.1, p. 1
notes.evidence: This part implements the Telemarketing and Consumer Fraud and Abuse Prevention Act

notes.front: What is the National Do Not Call Registry (DNC)?
notes.back: The registry the FTC maintains of people who do not wish to receive outbound telemarketing calls.
notes.explanation: Under the TSR, calling a number on the registry is an abusive practice unless the seller has written permission or an established business relationship.
notes.example: Like a "no junk mail" sign on a letterbox, but held centrally for telephone numbers.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 310 (Telemarketing Sales Rule), 2026 edition, § 310.4(b)(1)(iii)(B), p. 9
notes.evidence: That person’s telephone number is on the ‘‘do-not-call’’ registry, maintained by the Commission, of persons who do not wish to receive outbound

notes.front: What is the Telephone Consumer Protection Act (TCPA)?
notes.back: The 1991 federal law, codified at 47 U.S.C. 227, that restricts autodialled and prerecorded calls, unsolicited faxes and telephone solicitations.
notes.explanation: Section 227 opens its restrictions on the use of automated telephone equipment by making certain calls and faxes unlawful.
notes.example: Like the TSR, but written by Congress into the Communications Act and applied by the FCC.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. 227 (Telephone Consumer Protection Act, as amended), notes and subsec. (b)
notes.evidence: the Telephone Consumer Protection Act of 1991 ( Public Law 102–243; 105 Stat. 2394)

notes.front: What is the Junk Fax Prevention Act (JFPA)?
notes.back: The 2005 Act (Pub. L. 109–21) that rewrote the TCPA's ban on sending unsolicited advertisements to fax machines.
notes.explanation: The amendment notes to section 227 record that Pub. L. 109–21 amended the fax prohibition in subsection (b)(1)(C) generally; its short title is recorded under 47 U.S.C. 609.
notes.example: Like a patch to the TCPA that deals only with the fax machine.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. 227 (Telephone Consumer Protection Act, as amended), amendment notes, 2005
notes.evidence: Subsec. (b)(1)(C). Pub. L. 109–21, §2(a), amended subpar. (C) generally.

notes.front: What is the CAN-SPAM Act (CAN-SPAM)?
notes.back: The Controlling the Assault of Non-Solicited Pornography and Marketing Act of 2003, the federal law on commercial email, at 15 U.S.C. chapter 103.
notes.explanation: CAN-SPAM is the short form of the Act's full title, which the statute itself gives as an alternative citation.
notes.example: Like the TSR, but for marketing email rather than sales calls.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 103 (CAN-SPAM Act), short title note
notes.evidence: may be cited as the 'Controlling the Assault of Non-Solicited Pornography and Marketing Act of 2003', or the 'CAN-SPAM Act of 2003'.

notes.front: Under CAN-SPAM, what is a commercial electronic mail message?
notes.back: An email whose primary purpose is the commercial advertisement or promotion of a commercial product or service.
notes.explanation: The test is the primary purpose of the message, so an email that mainly does something else falls outside the definition.
notes.example: Like a sale flyer, but delivered to an inbox: "20% off all shoes this weekend".
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 103 (CAN-SPAM Act), §7702(2)(A)
notes.evidence: means any electronic mail message the primary purpose of which is the commercial advertisement or promotion of a commercial product or service

notes.front: What is the Wireless Domain Registry?
notes.back: The FCC's list of domain names used for mobile-service email, which it keeps under rules CAN-SPAM required to curb unwanted mobile commercial messages.
notes.explanation: CAN-SPAM section 7712 told the FCC, consulting the FTC, to make rules protecting consumers from unwanted mobile service commercial messages.
notes.example: Like the National Do Not Call Registry, but listing mobile carriers' email domains instead of phone numbers.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 103 (CAN-SPAM Act), §7712(b)
notes.evidence: The Federal Communications Commission, in consultation with the Federal Trade Commission, shall promulgate rules within 270 days to protect consumers from unwanted mobile service commercial messages.

notes.front: What is customer proprietary network information (CPNI)?
notes.back: Information about the quantity, configuration, type, destination, location and amount of a customer's telecommunications use, available to the carrier only through that relationship.
notes.explanation: The definition also covers information in a customer's telephone bills, but excludes subscriber list information.
notes.example: Like your phone company's record of whom you called and for how long, rather than your listed name in a directory.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. 222 (privacy of customer information), §222(h)(1)
notes.evidence: information that relates to the quantity, technical configuration, type, destination, location, and amount of use of a telecommunications service subscribed to by any customer of a telecommunications carrier

notes.front: What is the Cable Communications Policy Act?
notes.back: The 1984 Act (Pub. L. 98–549) whose subscriber privacy section, 47 U.S.C. 551, governs how cable operators collect and disclose subscriber information.
notes.explanation: Section 551 was added by Pub. L. 98–549 in October 1984; the notes to 47 U.S.C. 609 give that Act its short title.
notes.example: Like a privacy notice law, but only for your cable television provider.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. 551 (protection of cable subscriber privacy), §551 source credit
notes.evidence: as added Pub. L. 98–549, §2, Oct. 30, 1984

notes.front: What is the Video Privacy Protection Act (VPPA)?
notes.back: The federal law (18 U.S.C. 2710) making a video tape service provider liable if it knowingly discloses personally identifiable information about a consumer.
notes.explanation: Liability attaches to the knowing disclosure itself, and the aggrieved person may sue for the relief the section provides.
notes.example: Like a doctor's duty of confidence, but about which films you rented or bought.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. 2710 (Video Privacy Protection Act), §2710(b)(1)
notes.evidence: A video tape service provider who knowingly discloses, to any person, personally identifiable information concerning any consumer of such provider shall be liable to the aggrieved person

notes.front: What is the Driver's Privacy Protection Act (DPPA)?
notes.back: The 1994 federal law barring state motor vehicle departments from knowingly disclosing personal information from motor vehicle records, except as permitted.
notes.explanation: Section 2721(a) applies to the department and any officer, employee or contractor of it; permitted uses are listed in subsection (b).
notes.example: Like a lock on the licensing office's filing cabinet, with a list of who may hold a key.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 123 (Driver's Privacy Protection Act), §2721(a)
notes.evidence: A State department of motor vehicles, and any officer, employee, or contractor thereof, shall not knowingly disclose or otherwise make available to any person or entity

notes.front: Under the TSR, what counts as telemarketing?
notes.back: A plan, programme or campaign to induce purchases or charitable contributions by telephone, involving more than one interstate telephone call.
notes.explanation: A single interstate call does not make a campaign; the definition needs more than one.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 310 (Telemarketing Sales Rule), 2026 edition, § 310.2(ii), p. 4
notes.evidence: Telemarketing means a plan, program, or campaign which is conducted to induce the purchase of goods or services or a charitable contribution, by use of one or more telephones and which involves more than one interstate telephone call.

notes.front: Under the TSR, may a telemarketer call someone who told that seller not to call again?
notes.back: No. Calling a person who has said they do not wish to receive calls from that seller is an abusive practice.
notes.explanation: This entity-specific request binds calls made by or on behalf of that seller, whether or not the number is on the national registry.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 310 (Telemarketing Sales Rule), 2026 edition, § 310.4(b)(1)(iii)(A), p. 9
notes.evidence: That person previously has stated that he or she does not wish to receive an outbound telephone call made by or on behalf of the seller whose goods or services are being offered

notes.front: Under the TSR, what written permission lets a seller call a number on the National Do Not Call Registry?
notes.back: The person's express written agreement to receive that seller's calls, including the telephone number and the person's signature.
notes.explanation: The agreement must clearly show the person authorises calls by or on behalf of a specific party.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 310 (Telemarketing Sales Rule), 2026 edition, § 310.4(b)(1)(iii)(B)(1), p. 10
notes.evidence: Such written agreement shall clearly evidence such person’s authorization that calls made by or on behalf of a specific party may be placed to that person, and shall include the telephone number to which the calls may be placed and the signature

notes.front: Besides written permission, what else lets a seller call a number on the do-not-call registry under the TSR?
notes.back: An established business relationship with the person, provided the person has not asked that seller not to call.
notes.explanation: The relationship exception gives way to an entity-specific request: once the person says "don't call", it no longer helps.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 310 (Telemarketing Sales Rule), 2026 edition, § 310.4(b)(1)(iii)(B)(2), p. 10
notes.evidence: Can demonstrate that the seller has an established business relationship with such person, and that person has not stated that he or she does not wish to receive outbound telephone calls

notes.front: A TSR established business relationship arises from a purchase, rental, lease or financial transaction with the seller within the {{c1::540}} days before the call.
notes.explanation: A second, shorter window applies when the person only made an inquiry or application.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 310 (Telemarketing Sales Rule), 2026 edition, § 310.2(q)(1), p. 2
notes.evidence: The person’s purchase, rental, or lease of the seller’s goods or services or a financial transaction between the person and seller, within the 540 days

notes.front: Under the TSR, an inquiry or application about the seller's goods or services creates an established business relationship for {{c1::90}} days.
notes.explanation: The window runs over the days immediately before the date of the telemarketing call.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 310 (Telemarketing Sales Rule), 2026 edition, § 310.2(q)(2), p. 3
notes.evidence: The person’s inquiry or application regarding a good or service offered by the seller, within the 90 days

notes.front: Without prior consent, the TSR bars telemarketing calls to a residence outside {{c1::8:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m.}}, local time at the called person's location.
notes.explanation: The hours are measured where the called person is, not where the telemarketer sits.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 310 (Telemarketing Sales Rule), 2026 edition, § 310.4(c), p. 11
notes.evidence: outbound telephone calls to a person’s residence at any time other than between 8:00 a.m. and 9:00 p.m. local time at the called person’s location

notes.front: Under the TSR, when is an outbound call "abandoned"?
notes.back: When a person answers and the telemarketer does not connect a sales representative within two seconds of the person's completed greeting.
notes.explanation: Abandoning a call is itself listed as an abusive practice, subject to a safe harbour.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 310 (Telemarketing Sales Rule), 2026 edition, § 310.4(b)(1)(iv), p. 10
notes.evidence: if a person answers it and the telemarketer does not connect the call to a sales representative within two (2) seconds of the person’s completed greeting

notes.front: The TSR call abandonment safe harbour needs technology that abandons no more than {{c1::three per cent}} of calls answered by a person, per campaign or 30-day period.
notes.back: three per cent
notes.explanation: The safe harbour also requires ringing for 15 seconds or four rings, a recorded message and records proving compliance.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 310 (Telemarketing Sales Rule), 2026 edition, § 310.4(b)(4)(i), p. 11
notes.evidence: employs technology that ensures abandonment of no more than three (3) percent of all calls answered by a person

notes.front: Under the TSR, what must a seller have before placing a prerecorded sales message call?
notes.back: The recipient's express written agreement to receive that seller's prerecorded calls, with the person's telephone number and signature.
notes.explanation: The agreement must follow a clear and conspicuous disclosure that its purpose is to authorise prerecorded calls.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 310 (Telemarketing Sales Rule), 2026 edition, § 310.4(b)(1)(v)(A), p. 10
notes.evidence: the seller has obtained from the recipient of the call an express agreement, in writing

notes.front: Under the TSR, may a seller require agreement to prerecorded calls as a condition of buying?
notes.back: No. The agreement must be obtained without requiring it, directly or indirectly, as a condition of purchasing any good or service.
notes.explanation: An agreement extracted as the price of a purchase does not meet the rule.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 310 (Telemarketing Sales Rule), 2026 edition, § 310.4(b)(1)(v)(A)(ii), p. 10
notes.evidence: The seller obtained without requiring, directly or indirectly, that the agreement be executed as a condition of purchasing any good or service

notes.front: What must the TSR keypress opt-out in a prerecorded call do once used?
notes.back: Automatically add the number to the seller's entity-specific do-not-call list and immediately disconnect the call.
notes.explanation: It must be available at any time during the message.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 310 (Telemarketing Sales Rule), 2026 edition, § 310.4(b)(1)(v)(B)(ii)(A), p. 10
notes.evidence: Automatically add the number called to the seller’s entity-specific Do Not Call list; (2) Once invoked, immediately disconnect the call

notes.front: What caller identification details does the TSR require a telemarketer to transmit?
notes.back: The telephone number and, when the carrier makes it available, the telemarketer's name.
notes.explanation: The rule allows the seller's name and its customer service number, answered in business hours, to be substituted.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 310 (Telemarketing Sales Rule), 2026 edition, § 310.4(a)(8), p. 9
notes.evidence: Failing to transmit or cause to be transmitted the telephone number, and, when made available by the telemarketer’s carrier, the name of the telemarketer, to any caller identification service

notes.front: For the TSR do-not-call safe harbour, the seller must use a version of the registry obtained no more than {{c1::31}} days before the call.
notes.explanation: The seller must also keep records documenting the process it uses to scrub its calls.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 310 (Telemarketing Sales Rule), 2026 edition, § 310.4(b)(3)(iv), p. 11
notes.evidence: employing a version of the ‘‘do-not-call’’ registry obtained from the Commission no more than thirty-one (31) days prior to the date any call is made

notes.front: Under the TSR, a seller or telemarketer must keep its telemarketing records for {{c1::5 years}} from the date each record is produced, unless specified otherwise.
notes.back: 5 years
notes.explanation: Scripts and promotional material are kept for 5 years from when they stop being used.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 310 (Telemarketing Sales Rule), 2026 edition, § 310.5(a), p. 12
notes.evidence: Any seller or telemarketer must keep, for a period of 5 years from the date the record is produced unless specified otherwise

notes.front: What is the annual fee for National Do Not Call Registry data under the 2026 TSR text?
notes.back: $82 per area code, up to a maximum of $22,626; the first five area codes are free.
notes.explanation: The fee figures change over time, so check the current edition of the rule.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 310 (Telemarketing Sales Rule), 2026 edition, § 310.8(c), p. 16
notes.evidence: is $82 for each area code of data accessed, up to a maximum of $22,626; provided, however, that there shall be no charge to any person for accessing the first five area codes of data

notes.front: How does the TCPA define an automatic telephone dialing system?
notes.back: Equipment with the capacity to store or produce numbers to be called using a random or sequential number generator, and to dial them.
notes.explanation: Both elements appear in the definition: generating the numbers and dialling them.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. 227 (Telephone Consumer Protection Act, as amended), §227(a)(1)
notes.evidence: means equipment which has the capacity- (A) to store or produce telephone numbers to be called, using a random or sequential number generator; and (B) to dial such numbers

notes.front: Under the TCPA, when may an autodialled or artificial-voice call be made to a mobile phone number?
notes.back: For emergency purposes or with the prior express consent of the called party.
notes.explanation: The same rule covers emergency lines, hospital and care-home rooms and paging services.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. 227 (Telephone Consumer Protection Act, as amended), §227(b)(1)(A)
notes.evidence: (other than a call made for emergency purposes or made with the prior express consent of the called party) using any automatic telephone dialing system or an artificial or prerecorded voice

notes.front: What does the TCPA say about prerecorded-voice calls to a residential line?
notes.back: They need the called party's prior express consent, unless for emergencies, collecting a federally owed debt, or exempted by the FCC.
notes.explanation: The residential rule turns on the artificial or prerecorded voice, not on how the number was dialled.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. 227 (Telephone Consumer Protection Act, as amended), §227(b)(1)(B)
notes.evidence: to initiate any telephone call to any residential telephone line using an artificial or prerecorded voice to deliver a message without the prior express consent of the called party

notes.front: Under the TCPA as amended by the JFPA, what relationship allows an unsolicited fax advertisement?
notes.back: An established business relationship between sender and recipient, where the fax number was obtained in the permitted ways.
notes.explanation: The number must come from the recipient within that relationship, or from a directory or site where the recipient agreed to publish it.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. 227 (Telephone Consumer Protection Act, as amended), §227(b)(1)(C)
notes.evidence: an unsolicited advertisement, unless- (i) the unsolicited advertisement is from a sender with an established business relationship with the recipient

notes.front: Where must the opt-out notice appear on an unsolicited fax advertisement?
notes.back: Clearly and conspicuously on the first page.
notes.explanation: The notice must also say that failing to honour an opt-out request within the time set by the FCC is unlawful.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. 227 (Telephone Consumer Protection Act, as amended), §227(b)(2)(D)(i)
notes.evidence: the notice is clear and conspicuous and on the first page of the unsolicited advertisement

notes.front: A TCPA private action may recover actual monetary loss or {{c1::$500}} in damages for each violation, whichever is greater.
notes.explanation: The person may also seek an injunction, or both remedies together.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. 227 (Telephone Consumer Protection Act, as amended), §227(b)(3)
notes.evidence: to recover for actual monetary loss from such a violation, or to receive $500 in damages for each such violation, whichever is greater

notes.front: How far may a court increase TCPA damages for a wilful or knowing violation?
notes.back: To not more than three times the amount otherwise available.
notes.explanation: The increase is in the court's discretion; it is not automatic.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. 227 (Telephone Consumer Protection Act, as amended), §227(b)(3)
notes.evidence: increase the amount of the award to an amount equal to not more than 3 times the amount available under subparagraph (B) of this paragraph

notes.front: Who may sue under the TCPA's do-not-call rules?
notes.back: A person who received more than one call within any 12-month period by or for the same entity in violation of the rules.
notes.explanation: A single unlawful call is not enough for this private action.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. 227 (Telephone Consumer Protection Act, as amended), §227(c)(5)
notes.evidence: A person who has received more than one telephone call within any 12-month period by or on behalf of the same entity in violation of the regulations

notes.front: Is a transactional or relationship message a commercial electronic mail message under CAN-SPAM?
notes.back: No. The definition expressly excludes transactional or relationship messages.
notes.explanation: Such messages still may not carry materially false or misleading header information.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 103 (CAN-SPAM Act), §7702(2)(B)
notes.evidence: The term "commercial electronic mail message" does not include a transactional or relationship message.

notes.front: What does CAN-SPAM forbid in the header of a commercial or transactional email?
notes.back: Header information that is materially false or materially misleading.
notes.explanation: The ban covers transactional or relationship messages as well as commercial ones.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 103 (CAN-SPAM Act), §7704(a)(1)
notes.evidence: header information that is materially false or materially misleading

notes.front: When is a subject line unlawful under CAN-SPAM?
notes.back: When the sender knows it would likely mislead a reasonable recipient about a material fact regarding the message's contents or subject matter.
notes.explanation: Knowledge may be actual or fairly implied from objective circumstances.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 103 (CAN-SPAM Act), §7704(a)(2)
notes.evidence: that a subject heading of the message would be likely to mislead a recipient, acting reasonably under the circumstances, about a material fact regarding the contents or subject matter of the message

notes.front: A CAN-SPAM opt-out address or mechanism must keep working for no less than {{c1::30 days}} after the original message is sent.
notes.back: 30 days
notes.explanation: It must be functioning and clearly and conspicuously displayed.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 103 (CAN-SPAM Act), §7704(a)(3)(A)(ii)
notes.evidence: remains capable of receiving such messages or communications for no less than 30 days after the transmission of the original message

notes.front: Once a recipient opts out, CAN-SPAM bars further commercial email within the request's scope sent more than {{c1::10 business days}} after receipt.
notes.back: 10 business days
notes.explanation: The bar also reaches people sending on the sender's behalf who know the message falls within the request.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 103 (CAN-SPAM Act), §7704(a)(4)(A)
notes.evidence: more than 10 business days after the receipt of such request, of a commercial electronic mail message that falls within the scope of the request

notes.front: Under CAN-SPAM, what must a commercial email say about its own nature?
notes.back: It must clearly and conspicuously identify itself as an advertisement or solicitation.
notes.explanation: This one requirement falls away if the recipient gave prior affirmative consent.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 103 (CAN-SPAM Act), §7704(a)(5)(A)(i)
notes.evidence: clear and conspicuous identification that the message is an advertisement or solicitation

notes.front: What notice about refusing future mail must every commercial email carry under CAN-SPAM?
notes.back: Clear and conspicuous notice of the opportunity to decline further commercial email from the sender.
notes.explanation: The notice points to the return address or mechanism the Act requires.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 103 (CAN-SPAM Act), §7704(a)(5)(A)(ii)
notes.evidence: clear and conspicuous notice of the opportunity under paragraph (3) to decline to receive further commercial electronic mail messages from the sender

notes.front: What contact detail of the sender must every commercial email include under CAN-SPAM?
notes.back: A valid physical postal address of the sender.
notes.explanation: It is listed alongside the advertisement identifier and the opt-out notice.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 103 (CAN-SPAM Act), §7704(a)(5)(A)(iii)
notes.evidence: a valid physical postal address of the sender

notes.front: How does the FTC enforce CAN-SPAM?
notes.back: As if a violation were an unfair or deceptive act or practice under a rule made under the FTC Act.
notes.explanation: Other agencies enforce the Act for banks and some other regulated sectors instead.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 103 (CAN-SPAM Act), §7706(a)
notes.evidence: this chapter shall be enforced by the Commission as if the violation of this chapter were an unfair or deceptive act or practice
uses: unfair or deceptive acts or practices

notes.front: Which private party does CAN-SPAM expressly allow to sue?
notes.back: A provider of Internet access service adversely affected by certain violations.
notes.explanation: The enforcement section names the FTC, other agencies, states and access providers; it gives no action to individual recipients.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 103 (CAN-SPAM Act), §7706(g)(1)
notes.evidence: A provider of Internet access service adversely affected by a violation of section 7704(a)(1), (b), or (d) of this title

notes.front: Without customer approval, for what may a carrier use individually identifiable CPNI?
notes.back: Only to provide the telecommunications service it came from, or services necessary to or used in providing it.
notes.explanation: Uses required by law are also allowed, and publishing directories counts as a necessary service.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. 222 (privacy of customer information), §222(c)(1)
notes.evidence: Except as required by law or with the approval of the customer, a telecommunications carrier that receives or obtains customer proprietary network information by virtue of its provision of a telecommunications service shall only use, disclose, or permit access to

notes.front: What are two purposes for which a carrier may use CPNI without approval under 47 U.S.C. 222(d)?
notes.back: Among others: billing and collecting for its services, and protecting against fraudulent or unlawful use of them.
notes.explanation: Emergency location information and customer-initiated inbound calls are also listed.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. 222 (privacy of customer information), §222(d)
notes.evidence: to initiate, render, bill, and collect for telecommunications services; (2) to protect the rights or property of the carrier

notes.front: Which Act added the CPNI section, 47 U.S.C. 222, to the Communications Act?
notes.back: The Telecommunications Act of 1996 (Pub. L. 104–104).
notes.explanation: The section's source credit shows it was added by Pub. L. 104–104 in February 1996; the notes to 47 U.S.C. 609 give that Act its short title.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. 222 (privacy of customer information), §222 source credit
notes.evidence: as added Pub. L. 104–104, title VII, §702, Feb. 8, 1996

notes.front: When must a cable operator give subscribers its privacy notice?
notes.back: When entering the service agreement and at least once a year after that, as a separate written statement.
notes.explanation: The notice covers what is collected, its use and disclosure, retention, access and the subscriber's rights.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. 551 (protection of cable subscriber privacy), §551(a)(1)
notes.evidence: At the time of entering into an agreement to provide any cable service or other service to a subscriber and at least once a year thereafter, a cable operator shall provide notice in the form of a separate, written statement

notes.front: What does a cable operator generally need before disclosing subscriber personally identifiable information?
notes.back: The subscriber's prior written or electronic consent.
notes.explanation: Exceptions include disclosures needed to render the service and some name-and-address lists with an opt-out.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. 551 (protection of cable subscriber privacy), §551(c)(1)
notes.evidence: a cable operator shall not disclose personally identifiable information concerning any subscriber without the prior written or electronic consent of the subscriber concerned

notes.front: What minimum damages may a court award for a cable privacy violation under section 551(f)?
notes.back: Liquidated damages of $100 a day for each day of violation or $1,000, whichever is higher.
notes.explanation: Punitive damages and reasonable legal costs may also be awarded.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. 551 (protection of cable subscriber privacy), §551(f)(2)
notes.evidence: actual damages but not less than liquidated damages computed at the rate of $100 a day for each day of violation or $1,000, whichever is higher

notes.front: Under the VPPA, what is personally identifiable information?
notes.back: It includes information identifying a person as having requested or obtained specific video materials or services from a video tape service provider.
notes.explanation: The definition says "includes", so it is not a closed list.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. 2710 (Video Privacy Protection Act), §2710(a)(3)
notes.evidence: the term "personally identifiable information" includes information which identifies a person as having requested or obtained specific video materials or services from a video tape service provider

notes.front: In what form must VPPA consent to disclosure be given?
notes.back: Informed, written consent, which may be given electronically over the Internet, in a form distinct and separate from other legal or financial obligations.
notes.explanation: The consumer must also be offered a clear and conspicuous way to withdraw.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. 2710 (Video Privacy Protection Act), §2710(b)(2)(B)
notes.evidence: to any person with the informed, written consent (including through an electronic means using the Internet) of the consumer that- (i) is in a form distinct and separate from any form setting forth other legal or financial obligations of the consumer

notes.front: For how long can VPPA consent given in advance last?
notes.back: For a set period of no more than 2 years, or until the consumer withdraws it, whichever is sooner.
notes.explanation: At the consumer's choice, consent may instead be given at the time disclosure is sought.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. 2710 (Video Privacy Protection Act), §2710(b)(2)(B)(ii)
notes.evidence: is given in advance for a set period of time, not to exceed 2 years or until consent is withdrawn by the consumer, whichever is sooner

notes.front: What VPPA consent rule did the amendment by Pub. L. 112–258 replace?
notes.back: Written consent given only at the time the disclosure is sought.
notes.explanation: The amendment struck the old consent clause and added the current one, which allows electronic and advance consent.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. 2710 (Video Privacy Protection Act), amendment notes
notes.evidence: Pub. L. 112–258 added subpar. (B) and struck out former subpar. (B) which read as follows: "to any person with the informed, written consent of the consumer given at the time the disclosure is sought;"

notes.front: A court may award VPPA damages of actual damages but not less than liquidated damages of {{c1::$2,500}}.
notes.explanation: Punitive damages, legal costs and equitable relief are also available.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. 2710 (Video Privacy Protection Act), §2710(c)(2)
notes.evidence: actual damages but not less than liquidated damages in an amount of $2,500; (B) punitive damages

notes.front: Under the DPPA, which driving-related information is outside "personal information"?
notes.back: Information on vehicular accidents, driving violations and driver's status.
notes.explanation: The definition does include name, address, photograph, social security number and medical or disability information.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 123 (Driver's Privacy Protection Act), §2725(3)
notes.evidence: but does not include information on vehicular accidents, driving violations, and driver's status

notes.front: When may a state release motor vehicle records for bulk marketing under the DPPA?
notes.back: Only if the state has obtained the express consent of the person the information concerns.
notes.explanation: Express consent means consent in writing, which may be given electronically with an electronic signature.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 123 (Driver's Privacy Protection Act), §2721(b)(12)
notes.evidence: For bulk distribution for surveys, marketing or solicitations if the State has obtained the express consent of the person to whom such personal information pertains.

notes.front: For which insurance activities does the DPPA permit use of motor vehicle record information?
notes.back: Claims investigation, antifraud activities, rating or underwriting.
notes.explanation: Insurers, insurance support organisations and self-insured entities may use it for those activities.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 123 (Driver's Privacy Protection Act), §2721(b)(6)
notes.evidence: For use by any insurer or insurance support organization, or by a self-insured entity, or its agents, employees, or contractors, in connection with claims investigation activities, antifraud activities, rating or underwriting.

notes.front: What minimum damages may a court award in a DPPA civil action?
notes.back: Actual damages, but not less than liquidated damages of $2,500.
notes.explanation: Punitive damages need proof of wilful or reckless disregard of the law.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 123 (Driver's Privacy Protection Act), §2724(b)
notes.evidence: actual damages, but not less than liquidated damages in the amount of $2,500; (2) punitive damages upon proof of willful or reckless disregard of the law

notes.front: How does California's consumer privacy statute describe advertising targeted from a consumer's activity on other businesses' sites and apps?
notes.back: Targeting ads using personal information from activity across businesses, sites, apps or services other than the one the consumer intentionally interacts with.
notes.explanation: The statute calls this "cross-context behavioral advertising"; the line is drawn at the service the consumer chose to use.
notes.source: California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018 (Civ. Code 1798.100 et seq.), as in force 1 Jan. 2026, § 1798.140(k), p. 23
notes.evidence: means the targeting of advertising to a consumer based on the consumer’s personal information obtained from the consumer’s activity across businesses, distinctly branded internet websites, applications, or services

notes.front: A telemarketer in New York calls a consumer's home in California at 7:30 p.m. New York time (4:30 p.m. in California), without prior consent. Under the TSR calling-hours rule, is this allowed?
notes.back: B: yes, because it is 4:30 p.m. at the called person's location.
notes.choices:
A) No, because it is after 7 p.m. where the caller is
B) Yes, because it is 4:30 p.m. at the called person's location
C) No, calls to residences always need prior consent
D) Yes, because the calling-hours rule only applies to prerecorded calls
notes.choicesExplained: A: the rule measures time where the called person is. C: consent is needed only outside 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. D: the rule covers outbound calls generally.
notes.explanation: The TSR bars calls to a residence outside 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. local time at the called person's location.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 310 (Telemarketing Sales Rule), 2026 edition, § 310.4(c), p. 11
notes.evidence: at any time other than between 8:00 a.m. and 9:00 p.m. local time at the called person’s location

notes.front: A customer tells a gym chain's telemarketer "please never call me again". The number is not on the national registry. The gym's campaign calls again next month. What is the position under the TSR?
notes.back: C: it is an abusive practice, because she asked that seller not to call.
notes.choices:
A) Lawful, because the number is not on the national registry
B) Lawful, because she is an existing customer
C) An abusive practice, because she asked that seller not to call
D) Lawful if the call is placed by a different telemarketing firm
notes.choicesExplained: A: entity-specific requests apply regardless of the registry. B: an established relationship does not override a do-not-call request. D: the rule covers calls made on the seller's behalf, whoever places them.
notes.explanation: The TSR bans calls to a person who has said they do not want calls from or for that seller.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 310 (Telemarketing Sales Rule), 2026 edition, § 310.4(b)(1)(iii)(A), p. 9
notes.evidence: That person previously has stated that he or she does not wish to receive an outbound telephone call made by or on behalf of the seller

notes.front: A consumer on the National Do Not Call Registry asked a solar company for a quote 120 days ago and has bought nothing. Can the company rely on an established business relationship to call her?
notes.back: D: no, because an inquiry counts only for 90 days.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, the relationship lasts 540 days from any contact
B) Yes, registry numbers may be called once a quote is requested
C) No, registered numbers can never be called
D) No, because an inquiry counts only for 90 days
notes.choicesExplained: A: 540 days applies to purchases, rentals, leases or financial transactions. B: an inquiry helps only within its 90-day window. C: written agreement or a live relationship can still allow calls.
notes.explanation: An inquiry or application creates a relationship only within the 90 days before the call.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 310 (Telemarketing Sales Rule), 2026 edition, § 310.2(q)(2), p. 3
notes.evidence: The person’s inquiry or application regarding a good or service offered by the seller, within the 90 days

notes.front: An online shop makes customers tick a box agreeing to prerecorded sales calls before they can check out. It then places prerecorded sales calls to them. Is the agreement valid under the TSR?
notes.back: A: no, it was required as a condition of purchase.
notes.choices:
A) No, it was required as a condition of purchase
B) Yes, a ticked box is an express written agreement
C) Yes, any existing customer may receive prerecorded calls
D) No, prerecorded sales calls are banned outright
notes.choicesExplained: B: whatever its form, the agreement fails if purchase depends on it. C: customers still must give a valid agreement. D: prerecorded calls are allowed with a valid agreement.
notes.explanation: The agreement must be obtained without requiring it, directly or indirectly, as a condition of purchase.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 310 (Telemarketing Sales Rule), 2026 edition, § 310.4(b)(1)(v)(A)(ii), p. 10
notes.evidence: The seller obtained without requiring, directly or indirectly, that the agreement be executed as a condition of purchasing any good or service

notes.front: Which of these is telemarketing under the TSR definition?
notes.back: B: a campaign of interstate calls urging people to donate to a charity.
notes.choices:
A) One interstate call to a single friend about a sofa
B) A campaign of interstate calls urging people to donate to a charity
C) A yearly catalogue mailing, with the seller only taking calls
D) A letter asking for donations, with no calls
notes.choicesExplained: A: telemarketing needs a plan or campaign with more than one interstate call. C: the definition excludes such catalogue sales where the seller does not solicit by phone. D: there is no telephone use at all.
notes.explanation: Telemarketing covers campaigns to induce purchases or charitable contributions by telephone involving more than one interstate call.
notes.source: 16 CFR part 310 (Telemarketing Sales Rule), 2026 edition, § 310.2(ii), p. 4
notes.evidence: which is conducted to induce the purchase of goods or services or a charitable contribution, by use of one or more telephones and which involves more than one interstate telephone call

notes.front: A debt buyer uses an autodialler with a prerecorded voice to call consumers' mobile phones about a private (non-government) debt. The consumers never gave consent. What does the TCPA say?
notes.back: C: the calls are unlawful without prior express consent.
notes.choices:
A) Lawful, because debt collection is always exempt
B) Lawful, because the TCPA covers only landlines
C) Unlawful without prior express consent
D) Lawful if the calls are made in business hours
notes.choicesExplained: A: the residential-line exception is for debts owed to or guaranteed by the United States. B: section 227(b)(1)(A) expressly covers cellular telephone service. D: calling hours are no answer to missing consent.
notes.explanation: Autodialled or artificial-voice calls to mobile numbers need prior express consent unless made for emergencies.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. 227 (Telephone Consumer Protection Act, as amended), §227(b)(1)(A)
notes.evidence: made with the prior express consent of the called party) using any automatic telephone dialing system or an artificial or prerecorded voice

notes.front: A court finds a caller wilfully made 10 unlawful prerecorded calls to a consumer, who suffered no monetary loss. What is the most the court may award under the TCPA private action?
notes.back: D: $15,000, trebling $500 for each of the 10 calls.
notes.choices:
A) $500 in total
B) $1,500 in total
C) $5,000, with no power to increase it
D) $15,000, trebling $500 for each of the 10 calls
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: damages are $500 for each violation, not per case. C: wilful or knowing violations may be increased up to three times.
notes.explanation: The statute gives $500 per violation where that beats actual loss, and lets the court triple it for wilful or knowing violations.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. 227 (Telephone Consumer Protection Act, as amended), §227(b)(3)
notes.evidence: or to receive $500 in damages for each such violation, whichever is greater

notes.front: A supplier faxes a promotion to a long-standing customer who gave it their fax number. The fax has no opt-out notice. What is the problem under the TCPA as amended by the JFPA?
notes.back: A: the fax lacks the required opt-out notice on its first page.
notes.choices:
A) The fax lacks the required opt-out notice on its first page
B) Nothing: an established relationship removes all fax rules
C) Faxing advertisements is banned even to existing customers
D) Only the recipient's written invitation could make it lawful
notes.choicesExplained: B: the relationship exception still requires a compliant notice. C: an established business relationship can allow such faxes. D: the relationship route is an alternative to invitation or permission.
notes.explanation: The fax exception works only with a notice that is clear and conspicuous and on the first page.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. 227 (Telephone Consumer Protection Act, as amended), §227(b)(2)(D)(i)
notes.evidence: the notice is clear and conspicuous and on the first page of the unsolicited advertisement

notes.front: An airline emails a passenger's booking confirmation, with a small banner for hotel deals at the bottom. How is the email best classed under CAN-SPAM?
notes.back: B: a transactional or relationship message, as its primary purpose is confirming the booking.
notes.choices:
A) A commercial electronic mail message, because it contains an advertisement
B) A transactional or relationship message, as its primary purpose is confirming the booking
C) Outside CAN-SPAM altogether, so even false headers are allowed
D) A commercial message, because the passenger never consented
notes.choicesExplained: A: classification turns on the primary purpose, not any advertising content. C: transactional messages still may not carry false headers. D: consent is not the test for the category.
notes.explanation: Confirming a transaction the recipient agreed to is a listed transactional purpose, and such messages are not commercial electronic mail messages.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 103 (CAN-SPAM Act), §7702(17)(A)(i)
notes.evidence: to facilitate, complete, or confirm a commercial transaction that the recipient has previously agreed to enter into with the sender

notes.front: A subscriber unsubscribes from a retailer's promotional emails on a Monday. The retailer sends another promotion 14 business days later. What is the position under CAN-SPAM?
notes.back: C: it is unlawful, as more than 10 business days have passed.
notes.choices:
A) It is lawful, as the retailer has 30 days to act
B) It is lawful if the email repeats the opt-out link
C) It is unlawful, as more than 10 business days have passed
D) It is lawful because the subscriber once consented
notes.choicesExplained: A: 30 days is how long the opt-out mechanism must keep working, not the deadline to honour it. B: a new opt-out link does not cure the breach. D: the opt-out overrides earlier consent.
notes.explanation: Sending within the scope of an opt-out more than 10 business days after receiving it is unlawful.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 103 (CAN-SPAM Act), §7704(a)(4)(A)
notes.evidence: more than 10 business days after the receipt of such request

notes.front: A start-up's marketing email is honest, labelled as an advertisement and has a working unsubscribe link, but gives no postal address. Is it compliant with CAN-SPAM?
notes.back: D: no, it lacks a valid physical postal address.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, an email address is enough
B) Yes, postal addresses are needed only for sexually oriented mail
C) No, it must also carry the FTC's approval mark
D) No, it lacks a valid physical postal address
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Act asks for a physical postal address. B: the address rule applies to every commercial email. C: there is no FTC approval mark requirement.
notes.explanation: Every commercial email must give an identifier, an opt-out notice and a valid physical postal address.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 103 (CAN-SPAM Act), §7704(a)(5)(A)(iii)
notes.evidence: a valid physical postal address of the sender

notes.front: A retailer sends a promotional email with the subject line "Your account has been suspended" when nothing has happened to the account. Which CAN-SPAM rule is broken?
notes.back: A: the ban on deceptive subject headings.
notes.choices:
A) The ban on deceptive subject headings
B) The 10-business-day opt-out rule
C) The postal address requirement
D) None, because subject lines are not regulated
notes.choicesExplained: B: no opt-out request is involved. C: nothing suggests the address is missing. D: section 7704(a)(2) regulates subject headings.
notes.explanation: A subject line likely to mislead a reasonable recipient about a material fact about the message is unlawful.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 103 (CAN-SPAM Act), §7704(a)(2)
notes.evidence: a subject heading of the message would be likely to mislead a recipient, acting reasonably under the circumstances, about a material fact

notes.front: An individual who receives dozens of non-compliant marketing emails wants to sue the sender under CAN-SPAM. Which party does the Act's enforcement section expressly authorise to sue?
notes.back: B: an adversely affected provider of Internet access service.
notes.choices:
A) Any recipient of two or more unlawful emails
B) An adversely affected provider of Internet access service
C) Only the recipient's employer
D) Any competitor of the sender
notes.choicesExplained: A: that two-message pattern resembles the TCPA do-not-call action, not CAN-SPAM. C and D: neither is named in section 7706.
notes.explanation: Section 7706 lets the FTC, other agencies, states and adversely affected access providers enforce the Act.
notes.source: 15 U.S.C. chapter 103 (CAN-SPAM Act), §7706(g)(1)
notes.evidence: A provider of Internet access service adversely affected by a violation

notes.front: A mobile carrier wants to use subscribers' individual call-detail records to market an unrelated home-insurance product. What does 47 U.S.C. 222 require?
notes.back: C: the customers' approval, unless the law requires the use.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, as the carrier created the records
B) Only an annual privacy notice
C) The customers' approval, unless the law requires the use
D) A court order
notes.choicesExplained: A: the carrier's use is limited to providing the service the data came from. B: notice alone is not the test in section 222(c)(1). D: approval, not a court order, is the route for marketing.
notes.explanation: Without approval, individually identifiable CPNI may be used only for the service it came from and services necessary to provide it.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. 222 (privacy of customer information), §222(c)(1)
notes.evidence: Except as required by law or with the approval of the customer

notes.front: A privacy team is mapping which statute governs a phone carrier's call-detail records. Which enactment put the CPNI rules into the Communications Act?
notes.back: D: the Telecommunications Act of 1996.
notes.choices:
A) The Cable Communications Policy Act of 1984
B) The Telephone Consumer Protection Act of 1991
C) The CAN-SPAM Act of 2003
D) The Telecommunications Act of 1996
notes.choicesExplained: A: it added cable subscriber privacy, section 551. B: it added section 227 on calls and faxes. C: it governs commercial email.
notes.explanation: Section 222 was added by Pub. L. 104–104 in 1996.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. 222 (privacy of customer information), §222 source credit
notes.evidence: as added Pub. L. 104–104, title VII, §702, Feb. 8, 1996

notes.front: A cable operator wants to share subscribers' viewing histories with an advertising partner. What does section 551 generally require first?
notes.back: A: the subscribers' prior written or electronic consent.
notes.choices:
A) The subscribers' prior written or electronic consent
B) An opt-out chance in the annual notice
C) Nothing, if the partner is under contract
D) Approval from the FCC
notes.choicesExplained: B: an opt-out suffices only for name-and-address lists that reveal no viewing. C: a contract does not replace consent. D: section 551 turns on subscriber consent, not agency approval.
notes.explanation: A cable operator may not disclose subscriber personally identifiable information without prior written or electronic consent, subject to listed exceptions.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. 551 (protection of cable subscriber privacy), §551(c)(1)
notes.evidence: without the prior written or electronic consent of the subscriber concerned

notes.front: A streaming service shares which films each named user watched with a data broker, relying on a consent clause buried in its general terms of service. Under the VPPA, what is the flaw?
notes.back: B: consent must be in a form distinct and separate from other legal or financial obligations.
notes.choices:
A) None, because online consent is never valid
B) Consent must be in a form distinct and separate from other legal or financial obligations
C) None, if the terms were accepted
D) The VPPA covers only physical video tapes
notes.choicesExplained: A: the amended Act expressly allows consent through electronic means. C: consent buried in other terms fails the separate-form test. D: the Act covers similar audio visual materials, and consent rules apply to the provider here.
notes.explanation: VPPA consent must be informed, written (electronic allowed) and in a distinct and separate form.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. 2710 (Video Privacy Protection Act), §2710(b)(2)(B)(i)
notes.evidence: is in a form distinct and separate from any form setting forth other legal or financial obligations of the consumer

notes.front: A car dealer asks the state licensing office for all registered owners' names and addresses to mail a promotion. No owner has consented. What does the DPPA say?
notes.back: D: the state may not release the data for bulk marketing without express consent.
notes.choices:
A) The state may release it, as names and addresses are public
B) The state may release it if it charges a fee
C) The state may release it if the dealer promises not to resell
D) The state may not release the data for bulk marketing without express consent
notes.choicesExplained: A: names and addresses are personal information under the Act. B: a fee does not create a permitted use. C: a resale promise does not replace consent.
notes.explanation: Bulk distribution for surveys, marketing or solicitations needs the express consent of the person concerned.
notes.source: 18 U.S.C. chapter 123 (Driver's Privacy Protection Act), §2721(b)(12)
notes.evidence: For bulk distribution for surveys, marketing or solicitations if the State has obtained the express consent of the person to whom such personal information pertains.

notes.front: A news site shows a reader shoe ads because a tracking partner saw her browsing a separate shoe retailer's site. How does California's statute class this?
notes.back: A: cross-context behavioural advertising, as the data came from another business's site.
notes.choices:
A) Cross-context behavioural advertising, as the data came from another business's site
B) First-party advertising, because the news site shows the ads
C) Not advertising, because no purchase took place
D) Contextual advertising based only on the article
notes.choicesExplained: B: the targeting used activity on a different business's site. C: the definition turns on targeting, not purchases. D: the ads rest on her activity elsewhere, not the article.
notes.explanation: The definition covers targeting based on activity across businesses other than the one the consumer intentionally interacts with.
notes.source: California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018 (Civ. Code 1798.100 et seq.), as in force 1 Jan. 2026, § 1798.140(k), p. 23
notes.evidence: other than the business, distinctly branded internet website, application, or service with which the consumer intentionally interacts

notes.front: How do the minimum statutory damages under the VPPA and the Cable Act's section 551 differ?
notes.back: VPPA: $2,500 liquidated damages. Cable: $100 a day of violation or $1,000, whichever is higher.
notes.explanation: Both allow actual damages above those floors, punitive damages and legal costs.
notes.source: 47 U.S.C. 551 (protection of cable subscriber privacy), §551(f)(2)
notes.evidence: liquidated damages computed at the rate of $100 a day for each day of violation or $1,000, whichever is higher
